text: Blue-Green Biodiversity (BGB) initiative Molecular tools are an indispensable part of ecology and biodiversity sciences and implemented across all biomes. About a decade ago, the use and implementation of environmental DNA (eDNA) to detect biodiversity signals extracted from environ- mental samples opened new avenues of research. Initial eDNA research focused on understanding population dynamics of target species. Its scope thereafter broad- ened, uncovering previously unrecorded biodiversity via metabarcoding in both well-studied and understudied ecosystems across all taxonomic groups. The ap- plication of eDNA rapidly became an established part of biodiversity research, and a research field by its own. Here, we revisit key expectations made in a land-mark special issue on eDNA in Molecular Ecology in 2012 to frame the development in six key areas: (1) sample collection, (2) primer development, (3) biomonitoring, (4) quantification, (5) behaviour of DNA in the environment and (6) reference data- base development. We pinpoint the success of eDNA, yet also discuss shortfalls and expectations not met, highlighting areas of research priority and identify the unexpected developments. In parallel, our retrospective couples a screening of the peer-reviewed literature with a survey of eDNA users including academics, end- users and commercial providers, in which we address the priority areas to focus research efforts to advance the field of eDNA. With the rapid and ever-increasing pace of new technical advances, the future of eDNA looks bright, yet successful applications and best practices must become more interdisciplinary to reach its full potential. Our retrospect gives the tools and expectations towards concretely K E Y W O R D S biomonitoring, eDNA behaviour, primers, quantification, reference database, sampling Molecular tools are an indispensable part of ecology and biodiver- sity sciences yet had focused on tissue and organismal samples for a long time. Especially for macro-organisms, DNA was largely collected from the organism itself. Contrastingly, microbiologists had already routinely studied microbial communities derived from environmental samples for several decades (Steffan et al., 1988), and ancient DNA had been used to explore trace DNA from extant species in ice cores (Willerslev et al., 2003, 2007). Nonetheless, the use of molecular tools for biodiversity surveys was still lim- ited. It was not until 2008 that Ficetola and colleagues developed a method to detect a species (i.e. Bull Frog, Rana catesbeiana) from DNA extracted from a water sample. In the years to follow, the number of detections of single species from environmental sam- ples increased rapidly, which, coupled with the emergence of Next Generation Sequencing (NGS), ushered in a new era, and with it, the term environmental DNA or ‘eDNA’. Here, we refer to eDNA as all DNA extracted from environmental samples, encompassing both organisms and shed or free DNA (Pawlowski, Apothéloz- Perret-Gentil, & Altermatt, 2020; Pawlowski, Apothéloz-Perret- Gentil, Mächler, et al., 2020), as defined in early use (Taberlet, As research on eDNA gained momentum, in 2012 the journal Molecular Ecology published the landmark ‘Environmental DNA’ Special Issue (Taberlet, Coissac, Hajibabaei, et al., 2012). It out- lined the state of the field of eDNA research, including the – at the time – current progress and applications, limitations and future applications. The focus of the articles ranged from well-developed fields such as microbial ecology (e.g. Barberán et al., 2012; Zinger et al., 2012), diet analysis (e.g. Pompanon et al., 2012) and soil DNA (e.g. Bienert et al., 2012; Hiiesalu et al., 2012) to those tech- nical limitations which would need considerably more develop- ment (e.g. NGS (Shokralla et al., 2012) or bioinformatics (Coissac Given the rapid development, the field has not only massively advanced since then, but also extended. Environmental DNA- based approaches are now broadly used in research, monitoring and implementation, including companies offering eDNA com- mercial services (Biggs et al., 2015; Blackman et al., 2022; Bruce et al., 2021 respectively). Here, we revisit the Molecular Ecology 2012 Special Issue (Taberlet, Coissac, Hajibabaei, et al., 2012) for a retrospective of the advances, reflecting the challenges outlined a decade ago and discussing how these fit into the current state of the field. We structure our article along six key areas identi- fied in 2012, and which are each prominent areas in the field of eDNA today, namely (1) sample collection, (2) primer design, (3) biomonitoring, (4) quantification, (5) behaviour of DNA in the en- vironment, and (6) reference database development. Additionally, we conducted and present a survey of almost 500 scientists and end-users of eDNA to contrast these six key areas in a more gen- The first, and often most crucial step in any eDNA study, is the col- lection of the sample. To ensure detection of the target species or community and minimisation of contamination between samples, sampling must be performed in the most efficient and suitable manner with appropriate equipment and standardised procedures.

text: As already highlighted in the 2012 Special Issue, collecting DNA from microbial communities was an established practice (Zinger et al., 2012). However, both adequate sampling volume and replica- tion were highlighted as issues with microbial eDNA studies which would also apply to macrobial eDNA (Andersen et al., 2012; Bienert et al., 2012; Epp et al., 2012; Yoccoz, 2012; Zinger et al., 2012). The Special Issue also highlighted the need to develop other facets: ex- traction protocols, contamination prevention workflows and DNA storage (Andersen et al., 2012; Epp et al., 2012). These aspects would play a crucial role in any standardisation of methods for sam- pling and sample processing and ensure a consistent application of Given the undeniable importance of correctly targeting DNA ampli- fication, in the 2012 Special Issue, the unspecific nature of an eDNA sample (i.e. composed of a mixture of target and non-target DNA), and the expected low concentration and high level of degradation of target DNA were of most concern (Pompanon et al., 2012). To enhance detection probability, early eDNA studies focused on short markers for which the copy number of intracellular sequences was high (e.g. rDNA or mitochondrial DNA; Epp et al., 2012; Hiiesalu et al., 2012). However, Coissac et al. (2012) acknowledged that ‘find- ing new primer pairs [...] that are suitable for particular environmen- tal applications is one of the major challenges of metabarcoding’. Too specific metabarcoding primer pairs can result in false absences (er- roneous non-detections), whereas the lack of specificity for qPCR primers can be the cause of false detections of target organisms.

text: Individual studies have further highlighted concerns for sample design raised in the 2012 Special Issue. These include the importance of suf- ficient sample replication, which has vastly improved in terrestrial environments (see Dickie et al., 2018; Osborne et al., 2011; van der Heyde et al., 2022), and the significance of sample volume in aquatic research, which became evident quickly and repeatedly highlighted over the last decade (Altermatt et al., 2023).

text: Considering aquatic environments, the sampling approach differs between lentic, lotic and marine environments due to the size of the water body and the physical movement of the water (Bruce et al., 2021). In terms of sample volume, initially <100 mL of water was used in conjunction with ethanol precipitation (Deiner et al., 2015) whereas now the field has predominantly moved to filtration, with 1–5 L commonly used volumes (Bruce et al., 2021).

text: However, recent evidence, suggests that even larger volumes are needed to prevent false absences. In all cases, the sampling volume has been often a pragmatic consensus on sampling and filtration techniques, filter sizes and subsequent extraction meth- ods and was not necessarily driven by a priori consideration on minimal sample number and volumes needed to reach a sufficient level of true positives and minimise false absences. Consequent, several studies have moved towards the filtration of higher vol- umes (e.g. 30–60 L, Cilleros et al., 2019; Couton et al., 2023; Pont et al., 2018; Valentini et al., 2016), which is partly the result of developments of filter types and on-site filtering equipment (e.g. peristaltic pumps). Similarly, sample collection in terrestrial en- vironment does not focus solely on microbial diversity, but also characterises frequently metazoans or plant communities in the wild (Kirse et al., 2021; van der Heyde et al., 2022). The need to adapt sampling protocols has triggered several experiments on this question and although no ‘one size fits all’ approach has been found, sample volumes have been optimised (van der Heyde et al., 2022). Primarily, consensus emerged that water sam- ples should be filtered immediately, either in the field or at a lab (Hinlo et al., 2017) followed by preservation with the addition of Longmire's solution, ethanol or being stored at −20°C (Hinlo et al., 2017; Spens et al., 2017). If not directly processed (e.g. DNA extraction), soil samples should ideally be kept cool, but the im- pact of preservation differs between taxonomic groups (Guerrieri et al., 2021). Furthermore, contamination prevention methods have greatly increased since 2012. text: Despite these significant advances in sampling strategies and downstream processes, the understanding of eDNA heteroge- neity in aquatic and terrestrial systems remains limited (see also Section 8). Studies showed substantial turnover between replicates in marine and riverine settings, even when sampling large volumes (Mächler et al., 2021; Stauffer et al., 2021), yet a relatively high ho- mogeneity in groundwater samples (Couton et al., 2023). Similarly, soil replicates may exhibit very different composition despite geo- graphical proximity (Hermans et al., 2022). While spatial and site replications have been commonly incorporated in sampling proto- cols, temporal replication is still rare. Due to the nature of eDNA, that is, the link between species detection and their ecology, temporal replication is advised (Bruce et al., 2021). Although our survey suggests the development of this area is sufficient, future studies will need to focus more strongly on the effect of spatio- temporal replications, linking it to the dynamics of eDNA within the environment, whilst also considering the possible autocorrela- tion this generates. Since the 2012 Special Issue researchers have recognised that sampling strategies must consider the organism's life cycles (e.g. Crustaceans; Crane et al., 2021), sampling should be spatially close to the habitat of interest (e.g. Reef fish; Antich et al., 2021) and consider migrations within or between habitats As the field of eDNA continues to expand, methodological and sampling developments have followed suit. Sample collection and lab filtration which was once the standard protocol have now moved to onsite collection and filtrations, for example enclosed Sterivex filter units and the mobile eDNA sampler as described by Thomas et al. Automated or passive samplers in aquatic environments have also unveiled new opportunities for long-term sampling strat- egies. text: Moreover, other factors can influence the amplification of target DNA, such as inhibition by humic acids or sediments in the sample (Stoeckle et al., 2017) or the number of PCR cycles (Kelly et al., 2019). These biases and the low con- centration of target template DNA found in eDNA samples can lead to poor DNA amplification and making them more prone to succumb to stochastic effects (Taylor et al., 2019). Currently there is no consensus on how to mitigate the effects of these complex and interacting biases (Hoorfar et al., 2004), therefore making PCR optimisation an important step in the eDNA workflow (Bohmann Despite the past progress, the rapid developments in eDNA protocols calls for certain methodological standards to ascertain the quality of the results. Some standards were established for sin- gle species qPCR (e.g. MIQE guidelines Bustin et al., 2009) but are absent for metabarcoding approaches. Validation of eDNA primers should also become an inherent part of primer design (Thalinger, Deiner, et al., 2021). For evaluation of primers and protocols, report- ing of ‘negative results’ and biases could move the field forward. In- situ validation is also needed as their results cannot be anticipated during study design (e.g. in silico PCR; mock community testing) and it can deliver important lessons for future studies (Braukmann et al., 2019). Further studies should focus on better understanding the combined effect of more elusive factors on amplification bias, like sample quality, DNA composition of the sample and the presence of PCR inhibitors (Hugerth & Andersson, 2017). Kayama et al. (2021) successfully tested the use of machine-learning algorithms to pre- dict amplification success of different species in mixed bulk sam- ples. Similar predictive models could help in assessing the efficacy of laboratory protocols and thus improve data interpretation. The differences in ampli- fication success of species in a mixture could be compensated by a drastic increase in sequencing depth (e.g. from ~25 million reads on Illumina MiSeq to ~8 billion reads on Illumina NovaSeq, which allows much higher sequencing depths per sample), allowing the detection of poorly amplified taxa (Braukmann et al., 2019). Similarly, the develop- ment of long-read sequencing could allow the use of a broader range of markers. Early metabarcoding studies were restricted in terms of the realtively short amplicon length that could be used (e.g. 2 × 300 bp for Illumina), however, newer technologies, such as the Oxford Nanopore platform, can sequence much larger fragments (Tedersoo et al., 2021) and have already been applied to eDNA studies (See Egeter et al., 2022). Additionally, as a more detailed understanding of the strengths, limitations and biases of metabarcoding is gained, stud- ies are beginning to recognise the potential of PCR-free approaches.

This is especially the case in Europe and North America, where a replacement of existing biomonitoring techniques is always challenged by the transitional costs. Contrastingly, eDNA-based biomonitoring seems to be much more fruitful and less resistant in areas where no previous data or monitoring programmes exist, and thus are not constrained or matched to existing data. Furthermore, for small-bodied bioindica- tors (e.g. diatoms; Apothéloz-Perret-Gentil et al., 2017; Pawlowski, Apothéloz-Perret-Gentil, et al., 2021; Pawlowski, Bonin, et al., 2021) and terrestrial microbiomes (Schloter et al., 2018) taxonomy-free approaches using the rare eDNA sequences are potential ways to identify indicators based on sequence diversity alone (Cordier et al., 2018; Keck et al., 2018). text: However, as eDNA is inherently a different form of sampling (e.g. represents both different taxonomic information and at a differ- ent spatial scale to traditional point-based biomonitoring), it should be integrated into existing monitoring schemes as such (Blackman et al., 2024), and not used to distinguish ‘true’ signals by comparing it to traditional methods. Environmental DNA allows monitoring ef- forts to be upscaled; spatially and temporally (Altermatt et al., 2020), to integrate cryptic or elusive species, to detect multiple organismal groups that are targeted with specific primers and to incorporate new indicator groups, for example, previously overlooked taxa or novel bioindicators (see Pereira-da-Conceicoa et al., 2021; Sagova- Mareckova et al., 2021). Therefore, the future biomonitoring with eDNA lies not in the replacement but in a reformation of biomon- itoring approaches, seeking opportunities in a new form of data and implemented by using standardised calibration experiments (with current methods) to ensure correct interpretation at all stages The need to assign a species' abundance or biomass value to eDNA remains a hot topic and has been consistently the focus of 1365294x, 0, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/mec.17355, Wiley Online Library on [17/04/2024]. Numerous studies inves- tigated both the support and limitations of using data derived from eDNA as proxy for species abundances (Yates et al., 2019, 2023).

text: Quantification of species abundance, particularly from metabar- coding studies, is still seen by the community as one of the most needed areas of research in the field of eDNA (Figure 2). For ex- ample, the mean copy number of sequences within a cell, the po- tential for intragenomic sequence variation (Nelson et al., 2019) and the presence of heteroplasmy (Ricardo et al., 2020) are often inadequately documented or completely unknown for certain or- ganisms. This lack of information is very valuable for marker choice and primer design, makes it challenging to mitigate copy number biases. To avoid this issue would entail the identification of a uni- versal, single-copy nuclear marker linked to a comprehensive ref- erence database. Unfortunately, this is currently unavailable and markers commonly targeted in biodiversity studies often have multiple copies, for amplification purposes, for example varia- tion in mitochondrial densities and the number of tandem repeats of markers (Andres et al., 2023), such as 18S and ITS, will create disparities in the numbers of reads between species in all stud- ies. Although some research groups, particularly those focusing on a limited number of target species, have attempted to address copy number variations by conducting quantitated qPCR analyses alongside metabarcoding studies, this approach is impractical for studies targeting biodiversity. This is coupled with two processes which mediate the relationship between a species' abundance and the quantification of its DNA in an environmental sample: first, the number of individuals and their eDNA concentration in the sample, which is influenced both by the species physiology and the state of the DNA being detected and second, that between eDNA con- centration and the output of quantification, either in copy number (qPCR) or read count (metabarcoding). For bacteria and fungi, cap- turing entire living organisms mitigates the first process, reduc- ing potential biases and leading to a wider acceptance of read or copy number as a reliable measure of species abundance (Smets et al., 2016). However, it is important to acknowledge that these groups have varying gene copy numbers (Vos et al., 2012), meaning a direct one-to-one comparison is not always applicable. In the case of metazoans, both processes are applicable, thus increasing possi- ble biases. Consequently, studies have demonstrated strong (Pilliod et al., 2013; Skelton et al., 2022; Takahara et al., 2013), weak (Evans et al., 2016) and no correlations (Deagle et al., 2013) between spe- cies abundance and read or copy number. Positive correlations are often constrained to a few specific taxonomic groups, particularly fish, and within closed habitats, such as mesocosms and natural or artificial ponds (Rourke et al., 2022). Conversely, reports of positive correlations between read or copy number and species abundance in other groups (e.g. invertebrates), different habitats (e.g. rivers) or other sample types (e.g. soil and air) are generally scarce.

text: Since 2012 many studies have tried to understand the factors potentially affecting the relationship between individual counts and read or copy numbers of sequences (Figure 1). These potential bi- ases are difficult to estimate and vary significantly across organisms and environments. This includes favouring species-specific methods (e.g. qPCR and ddPCR) whenever possi- ble, selecting low DNA transport sites (e.g. lentic water bodies), or targeting species with similar life history traits (Rourke et al., 2022;

filename: Molecular Ecology - 2024 - Blackman - Environmental DNA  The next chapter.pdf
text: Alternatively, improving species quantification can be achieved by distinguishing attempts that focus on within-sample, across-species comparisons versus those that concentrate on across- sample, within-species comparisons, each of which can be tackled with various sequencing and modelling techniques. Promising ap- proaches, like adding synthesised DNA (‘DNA spike-in’) or correction equations, have shown potential for improving abundance estimations (Luo et al., 2023; Spear et al., 2021; Ushio et al., 2018). Additionally, Pont (2023) recently suggested combining species-specific qPCR primer assays with metabarcoding to help quantify the total amount of amplified DNA. However, the efficacy of these approaches is still subject to caution. Furthermore, as these approaches may primarily reflect the number of cells rather than individuals, further research is required to address differences in both shedding rates and number of cells between species. While the Special Issue made assumptions that quantification would likely be possible, the research community remains divided on this, and that community-based quantification methods should, for now, primarily be constrained to single-cell or- ganisms, whose abundance estimations are more reliable.

text: The role of abiotic factors on DNA degradation for abundance es- timations in natural environments is therefore challenging (Hansen et al., 2018). The initial state of eDNA when captured also influences rates of its decay. For instance, decay occurs faster in longer than in shorter fragments (Jo et al., 2017), leading to variation in eDNA com- position over time. In this respect, sequential filtering with decreasing pore size (Brandão-Dias et al., 2023) and separation of eDNA states (Kirtane et al., 2023) show potential for increasing our understand- Despite the progress accomplished in the last decade, many un- certainties remain, hindering a full understanding of DNA behaviour and its subsequent detection. To address these uncertainties, there is a need to expand process-based models that jointly account for physical processes affecting eDNA dynamics in the environment (e.g. biotic and abiotic factors) and sequencing stochasticity (Carraro et al., 2020; Harrison et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2023). This will likely Reference databases were highlighted by the community survey as requiring the most development (Figure 2). Despite this critical view, there has been significant progress since 2012. This progress is not visible in the number of publications recorded in this time (Figure 1), which tended to focus on the gap analysis (e.g. Marques et al., 2021; Weigand et al., 2019). Instead, the most visible and easily quantifiable advancement is the constant effort made by scientists to complete the databases with new sequences and new taxa. For example, Genbank, the largest public repository for DNA data has seen its number of sequences increase from 151.8 to 242.5 mil- lion (+60%) during the last decade (https://​www.​ncbi.​nlm.​nih.​gov/​ genba​nk/​stati​stics/​). This surge in sequences is undeniably linked to better coverage of taxonomic diversity and better results at the taxonomic assignment stage (Stoeckle et al., 2020). A second major evolution regarding reference databases is the growing awareness that the quality of the data is as critical as its quantity (Blackman, Brantschen, et al., 2023; Keck, Couton, et al., 2022; Keck, Blackman, et al., 2022). Interestingly, there was relatively little discussion of this in 2012, perhaps because at the time, public data were not avail- able in such large amounts, or because the problem of poor-quality data had not yet been clearly identified by the scientific commu- nity. Furthermore, it was common to sequence reference data for each new study (Andersen et al., 2012; Bienert et al., 2012; Hiiesalu et al., 2012; Valentini et al., 2009), hence guaranteeing a better control on the reference data quality but at great cost and effort.

text: The fast-growing use of molecular approaches and the increasing need for quick and easy access to good quality reference data has prompted the development of many expert-curated databases avail- able for a variety of groups and markers (e.g. Blackman, Brantschen, et al., 2023; Decelle et al., 2015; Guillou et al., 2013; Morard et al., 2015; Mordret et al., 2018; Rimet et al., 2016). At the same time, a rich and mature software ecosystem has emerged to sup- port the development and curation of reference databases (Jeunen et al., 2023; Keck, Blackman, et al., 2022; Richardson et al., 2020).

filename: Molecular Ecology - 2024 - Blackman - Environmental DNA  The next chapter.pdf
text: Such reference curated and closed reference databases can be seen as the gold-standard, and often give the best and long-term track- able repeatability. Yet, given the extensive efforts involved, they are often kept closed to the research groups using them. Thus, as an alternative, many analyses are based on existing, open reference databases (GenBank, etc.). Their advantage is an often much larger coverage, yet at the cost of possible taxonomic or other errors. Also, and hitherto rather overseen, is the need to keep documentation of time-frozen exports of databases for the repeatability of analyses.

filename: Molecular Ecology - 2024 - Blackman - Environmental DNA  The next chapter.pdf
text: These open databases are constantly evolving, and thus the same analysis will result in different outcomes depending on the timepoint of data-export chosen. While this could prohibit long-term compara- bility, it also opens up the potential of re-analysing eDNA sequenc- ing data. While not yet identified as an opportunity in 2012, there is great potential in re-analysing older sequencing datasets with better contemporary databases, and also to get an understanding of the robustness of the findings with respect to database completeness.

text: Due to the unprecedented effort over the last 10 years to se- quence biodiversity, reference databases are now substantially more exhaustive and even include complete – or near to complete – references for some restricted taxonomic groups and geographi- cal areas (e.g. Blackman, Walser, et al., 2023; Dziedzic et al., 2023).

text: This is particularly important for taxonomic groups and geographical regions that are currently underrepresented in databases. Notably, several large-scale initiatives such as the International Barcode of Life project (iBOL; International Barcode of Life, 2010); BIOSCAN (Hobern & Hebert, 2019), Earth BioGenome (Lewin et al., 2022), European Reference Genome Atlas (Theissinger et al., 2023) and the Darwin Tree of Life (Darwin Tree of Life Project Consortium et al., 2022) are underway and signal a positive outlook for the en- richment of DNA reference databases around the world which will help to achieve comprehensive and accessible reference databases.

text: Environmental DNA has revolutionised the way in which biodiver- sity is detected and researched. In the relatively short time since Ficetola et al. (2008) published the detection of the Bullfrog, we have seen huge efforts in the development of techniques and ap- preciation of what can be achieved using eDNA. After more than a decade of research and implementation, many promises of the 2012 Special Issue came true, including an increase in the detection of bio- diversity and the potential implementation of biomonitoring for fish.

filename: Molecular Ecology - 2024 - Blackman - Environmental DNA  The next chapter.pdf
text: Contrastingly, novel challenges emerged, such as understanding the behaviour of eDNA and the influence of abiotic and biotic effects on the detection of a species, particularly when it comes to quantifica- tion of a species. Our literature screening revealed biases, some un- expected, to the publication of certain areas of the field. However, the survey consistently showed across all areas that participants felt the level of development needed was higher (categories 4 and 5) compared to little or no development needed (categories 1 and 2), highlighting our understanding of the processes influencing eDNA requires the most development, followed by reference database completion. Similarly, there remains a need to translate the findings of eDNA studies into practice as this survey comes at a time when the field of eDNA is moving from development to potential applica- tion. We therefore encourage the field of eDNA research to now focus on these under-researched areas and close these gaps in the decade to come. This will require a cross-disciplinary approach with integration from multiple players, namely ecologists, molecular sci- entists, earth scientists, hydrologists and modellers. Therefore, the next chapter of eDNA looks bright, collaborative and full of potential as we move towards understanding, interpreting and translating this work into practice for biodiversity research and conservation.
